analysis.one_liner: Limits tax deductions that companies which redomiciled abroad use to strip U.S. earnings.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in February 2016 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2017, with 5 Democratic sponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: When a U.S. company 'inverts' — moves its paper headquarters overseas — the remaining U.S. part can load up on debt owed to its own foreign parent and deduct the interest, shrinking its American taxable income. This bill tightens the existing rules for those companies: it would drop a debt-to-equity test, cut the share of income protected for interest deductions from 50% to 25%, and limit how long disallowed interest can be carried forward. The money saved would otherwise flow to the Treasury, which is funded by ordinary taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, in the form of a broader tax base: corporations related to inverted companies could no longer deduct as much interest paid to their own foreign affiliates, so more of their U.S. income would be taxed [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill applies the existing interest-deduction limits more strictly to corporations tied to 'inverted' companies, removing the debt-to-equity threshold that currently lets some of them escape the limit entirely [S2][S3].

It cuts the allowed net interest expense from 50% to 25% of adjusted taxable income and limits the carryforward of disallowed interest to five years, so less profit is deducted away on paper [S2][S3].
It covers not just inverted corporations themselves but any U.S. corporation in the same corporate family, closing the route of paying interest to the offshore parent [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations connected to inverted companies — the U.S. members of those groups would lose a large slice of interest deductions they now claim against U.S. income [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Inverted multinationals and their U.S. units

drawbacks.text: The bill targets only companies tied to inverted corporations, not other multinationals using the same debt-pushing techniques, so it is a narrow fix rather than a general rewrite of interest-deduction rules [S2][S3].

Critics of stricter interest limits generally argue they raise the after-tax cost of borrowing for the affected companies, which can mean less investment in U.S. operations and possibly higher prices; those effects are not addressed in the bill text.

Restricting deductions for foreign-owned structures can add compliance complexity and, in some economists' view, discourages foreign ownership of U.S. assets — trade-offs an honest supporter would have to weigh.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is straightforward: more tax revenue from a specific set of companies that moved their headquarters on paper but kept their business in the U.S., versus somewhat higher borrowing costs for those companies. The bill is well-aimed at the most visible avoidance pattern (inversion-related earnings stripping) but leaves the same tactic untouched for multinationals that never inverted.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never held a markup or brought it to the floor, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sander Levin introduced the bill on February 23, 2016, with four Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Van Hollen, Pascrell, Thompson, and Rangel [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means — the only action the bill ever received [S5].
The committee took up no further action, and no vote was ever held in either chamber before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies connected to inverted corporations are better off: they keep the full interest deductions the bill would have curtailed, and the Treasury forgoes the revenue. Nobody else gains from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Sander Levin
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-MI), bill sponsor and ranking member of the Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tighten interest-deduction limits on companies related to inverted corporations.

for.name: 4 of 188 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Reps. Van Hollen, Pascrell, Thompson, and Rangel).

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Democrats, no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died without action in the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee.

industries.industry: U.S. corporations related to inverted (offshore-redomiciled) companies
industries.note: The bill strips away a major deduction channel — interest paid to their own foreign parent — that reduces their U.S. taxable income. Their tax savings come at the expense of the broader taxpayer base that funds the Treasury.

industries.industry: U.S. tax advisory and accounting industry
industries.note: The industry earns fees designing and defending these debt structures; a stricter rule would cut demand for that work while raising compliance fees under the new regime. The sources do not address this industry directly; the effect follows from how the rules work.
